title: Homelessness payments tripled; the count of homeless people barely moved

beats.text: San Francisco’s homelessness department pays nonprofits to run shelters and housing.

visual.label: Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing
visual.sub: pays nonprofits to run shelter and housing

beats.text: In fiscal 2019, it paid them 158.9 million dollars.

visual.label: Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing
visual.sub: pays nonprofits to run shelter and housing

beats.text: By fiscal 2026, how much?

visual.label: Fiscal 2026

beats.text: 518.3 million dollars.

visual.label: paid to nonprofits, fiscal 2026

beats.text: This is a lead, not a finding.

visual.line: This is a lead, not a finding: a pattern in public records. This film says what the records show, what they do not show, and what would settle it.

beats.text: The spending’s stated goal is fewer homeless people.

visual.label: The goal: fewer homeless people

beats.text: On one night in 2019, the count was 8,035. And in 2026?

visual.label: The goal: fewer homeless people
people counted homeless, 2026

beats.text: Per person counted, the money went from 19,771 dollars to 65,011.

visual.label: paid to providers per person counted homeless, 2026

beats.text: Why didn’t the count fall? People keep becoming homeless.

beats.text: Part of the rise paid for hotel rooms and new housing after the pandemic. Those cost more per person than shelter.

visual.label: Hotel rooms and new housing

beats.text: And the money did buy things. Shelter beds grew from 3,403 to 4,837.

visual.label: Shelter and transitional beds

beats.text: Counting month by month, supportive-housing move-ins rose from 1,009 a year to 1,684.
That’s up 67 percent. Payments rose 226.
The City’s deduplicated count for fiscal 2026 is 1,767,

visual.label: Households moved into supportive housing, deduplicated (City scorecard)

beats.text: down from 1,965 in 2024.

visual.label: Households moved into supportive housing, deduplicated (City scorecard)

beats.text: Count every kind of housing, and the department’s own page gives 2,529 households

visual.label: Households moved into housing, fiscal 2025-26 (the department’s page)

beats.text: But of people assessed this fall, only 24 percent were sent to a housing referral.

visual.label: of those assessed, 1 Jul - 30 Sep 2026, sent to a housing referral

beats.text: Then the yardstick every city reports to HUD. Of people leaving shelter, how many reach a permanent home?

visual.label: Leaving shelter for a home

beats.text: 17.4 percent.

visual.label: left shelter for permanent housing, fiscal 2024
visual.sub: San Francisco’s own report to HUD

beats.text: Ten peer cities, from Los Angeles to New York, had a median of 35.8 percent.

visual.label: Leaving shelter for permanent housing, fiscal 2024

beats.text: San Francisco was the lowest of the 11.

visual.label: Leaving shelter for permanent housing, fiscal 2024

beats.text: Its own figure was 63.3 percent in 2018, but on 1,185 exits.
Not like for like: in 2024, 45.4 percent of shelter exits had an unknown destination.

visual.label: of shelter exits, fiscal 2024: destination unknown

beats.text: These aren’t our estimates. The City reported these counts to HUD itself.

visual.text: Counts through 2024 and the bed inventory are the figures San Francisco reported to HUD.

beats.text: What’s missing is which providers did well, and which didn’t. The City doesn’t publish results contract by contract.

cards: Which providers or programs performed poorly
That the count would not have been higher without the spending

beats.text: The 2022-23 Civil Grand Jury asked for exactly that: outcomes in every contract, and regular reporting.

visual.text: recommended consistent contract performance outcomes, contract-monitoring standards and regular homelessness reporting

beats.text: In 2025, the contracting office answered that it will not implement them. The department says it will, in the future.

visual.text: recommended consistent contract performance outcomes, contract-monitoring standards and regular homelessness reporting

beats.text: What would settle it? Results for each contract: placements, returns to homelessness, and cost per exit.

cards.what: Per-contract outcomes: placements, returns, cost per exit
The Controller’s and Budget and Legislative Analyst’s audits

beats.text: No audit has tied the spending to the count.
A lead is a question, not an accusation.
